items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place and they've been coughing all evening. You want to say, gently, "you should go to the hospital." Not a command, not "you must" — just solid, caring advice. That's exactly the job of ほうがいい.

The pattern means something like *had better* or *should*. You attach it to a verb and you're handing someone a recommendation: this choice is the better one. Here's the hospital line.

```jp
{{byouin||病[びょう]院[いん]}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}ほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should go to the hospital.*

Notice the verb is {{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}} — the past form — even though nothing has happened yet. That surprises everyone at first. Hold that thought; it's the whole trick of this pattern.

## How it works

There are two shapes, depending on whether you're recommending *doing* something or *not doing* it.

For "you should do X", take the plain past form of the verb (the た-form) and add ほうがいい.

```jp
{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}ほうがいいです。
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{yasumu|ta|休[やす]んだ}}ほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should take medicine.*
*You should rest today.*

Why the past form for future advice? Think of ほう as "the ~ side / the ~ option" (it's the same {{hou||方[ほう]}} you'll meet in comparisons). You're literally saying "the *having-taken-medicine* side is good" — you picture the action as already done and judge that outcome as the better one. The past form freezes the action into a completed picture you can weigh.

For "you should *not* do X", use the plain negative — the ない-form — and add ほうがいい. This one stays present, no past trickery.

```jp
{{sono||その}}{{osake||お酒[さけ]}}を{{nomu-v|nai|飲[の]まない}}ほうがいいです。
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{oyogu|nai|泳[およ]がない}}ほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not drink that alcohol.*
*You'd better not swim today.*

So the split is clean: **positive advice → past (た) + ほうがいい**, **negative advice → ない + ほうがいい**. That asymmetry looks odd but it's fixed and reliable.

You can make the whole thing more polite by keeping です on the end (ほうがいいです), or leave it off for plain speech (ほうがいい). And you can soften it further by tacking よ on the end, which makes it feel like a friendly heads-up rather than a verdict.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest trap is reaching for the plain *present* form on the positive side. {{iku-v||行[い]く}}ほうがいい isn't the natural advice pattern — for a specific recommendation to a specific person, you want {{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}ほうがいい.

> For concrete, in-the-moment advice ("you should go *now*"), use the past form: {{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}ほうがいい. The present form {{iku-v||行[い]く}}ほうがいい drifts toward general comparison ("going is the better option, in general") and sounds weaker as personal advice.

The negative side has no such split — it's always ない, never past.

```jp
{{takusan||たくさん}}{{taberu|nai|食[た]べない}}ほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not eat a lot.*

One more thing about tone: ほうがいい is genuinely stronger than a bare suggestion. When you say {{yasumu|ta|休[やす]んだ}}ほうがいい, you're implying there's a real downside to *not* resting. For a lighter "how about resting?" you'd reach for something else entirely (you already know {{dou||どう}}ですか for that). Save ほうがいい for when you mean it.

## Casual speech

Drop the です and you're already casual: {{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}ほうがいい. In fast speech people often shorten ほう to ほ and swallow the が, so ほうがいい can come out sounding like *ほうがいい* run together — you'll hear it, you don't need to produce it. The safe casual form is simply the plain one with よ:

```jp
{{hayai-early|stem|早[はや]く}}{{neru|ta|寝[ね]た}}ほうがいいよ。
```

*You'd better go to sleep early.*

That よ is doing a lot of work — it turns a flat statement into "hey, just so you know." Very common when you're looking out for a friend.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is かもしれない, *might / maybe*. They feel related but do opposite jobs. かもしれない reports a possibility; ほうがいい pushes a choice.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}かもしれません。
{{kasa||傘[かさ]}}を{{motsu|ta|持[も]った}}ほうがいいですよ。
```

*It might rain tomorrow.*
*You'd better take an umbrella.*

See how the first sentence just floats a possibility, and the second one leans in with a recommendation because of it. Swap them and it breaks: you can't advise with かもしれない, and ほうがいい can't merely speculate.

It also brushes up against と{{omou||思[おも]う}}, *I think that*. と{{omou||思[おも]う}} is your private opinion; ほうがいい is a recommendation aimed at the listener. "{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}は{{ii||いい}}と{{omou||思[おも]う}}" says what *you* feel; "{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}ほうがいい" tells the other person what to *do*. Same warmth, different direction.

## Closing

Recap: past (た) form for "you should," ない form for "you'd better not," both capped with ほうがいい — and add です or よ to set the tone. The past-tense-for-future-advice quirk is the one to burn in.

Hold onto the ない side of this pattern — that plain negative form is the same building block you'll need soon when we meet {{mada||まだ}}〜て{{iru-exist|nai|いない}}, "haven't done it yet."
caution_notes: For positive advice use the plain past (た) form: 行ったほうがいい, not 行くほうがいい.
For negative advice always use the plain negative (ない) form — never a past form.
ほうがいい is stronger than a casual suggestion; it implies a real downside to ignoring it, so save it for when you mean it.
Add です for politeness or よ for a friendly heads-up; the bare plain form is casual.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're looking out the window at a sky full of dark clouds. You don't have a weather report open, you're not psychic, but you do have an opinion — and you have to decide whether to grab an umbrella on the way out. Japanese has an ending built exactly for this moment: stating something you believe without claiming you're sure of it.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}でしょう。
```
*Tomorrow it'll probably rain.*

That's でしょう. Tack it onto the end of a sentence and a flat statement turns into an educated read on the situation — confident enough to say out loud, honest enough to admit you could be wrong.

## How it works

でしょう attaches to the plain form of whatever you're making a call about — the same plain form you already use in casual sentences, not the polite ます／です form. For a verb or an i-adjective, that part is easy: the plain form already ends the way it needs to, so でしょう just goes straight on afterward.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{mou||もう}}{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}でしょう。
```
*He's probably busy already.*

{{kare||彼[かれ]}} hasn't said anything, you haven't called him — you're just going off what you already know about his week.

Nouns and na-adjectives look almost the same, with one catch. On their own they'd need だ (the plain form of です) to close the sentence. でしょう doesn't stack on top of that だ; it takes its spot instead.

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}だ → {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}でしょう
```

Drop the だ, add でしょう, and you're done — no double copula, no leftover piece sitting in the middle.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{heya||部屋[へや]}}は{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}でしょう。
```
*This room is probably quiet.*

Same move with a plain noun: {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}} (rain) doesn't take だ before でしょう either, which is exactly what happened in the very first example above.

でしょう also shows up teamed with {{tabun||多[た]分[ぶん]}} (probably) at the front of the sentence. The two aren't redundant — {{tabun||多[た]分[ぶん]}} flags that a guess is coming, and でしょう is the ending that follows through on it.

```jp
{{tabun||多[た]分[ぶん]}}{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{yuki||雪[ゆき]}}でしょう。
```
*Tomorrow will probably be snow.*

## Rules and exceptions

でしょう is a read, not a report. It has to come from something you're piecing together yourself — what you can see, what you know, what seems likely — not something someone told you directly. Save that job for another pattern; more on that below.

It also undersells confidence you actually have, so don't reach for it out of habit. If the rain has already started outside your window, just say {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}です. Adding でしょう when you're not actually guessing at anything reads as strangely unsure of yourself.

There's a spoken trick worth knowing before you hear it and get thrown off, too. Say でしょう with your voice rising at the end, and it stops working as a guess. It becomes a check for agreement — closer to "isn't it?" than "I think so."

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{samui||寒[さむ]い}}でしょう？
```
*It's cold today, isn't it?*

> With rising intonation, でしょう isn't hedging anymore — it's fishing for a nod back from whoever's listening.

Falling intonation, same exact sentence, and you're back to a plain guess. Context and tone carry the whole difference; the words on the page never change.

## Casual speech

Among friends, でしょう shrinks down to だろう — same job, plainer register, the kind of ending that fits with {{boku||僕[ぼく]}} or {{kimi||君[きみ]}} far more comfortably than with a stranger or a teacher.

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}だろう。
```
*She's probably a teacher.*

だろう also pairs naturally with ね when you're thinking out loud and inviting whoever's next to you to agree, rather than stating a fact.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}だろうね。
```
*I bet tomorrow will be busy.*

Keep でしょう for anyone you'd address politely, and save だろう for people you'd already speak plainly to — the swap is entirely about who's listening, not about how sure you are.

## Contrast

You've already got によると for passing along someone else's information — Noun + によると, "according to X." That's a report: the information came from somewhere outside your own head.

```jp
{{shinbun||新[しん]聞[ぶん]}}によると{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}です。
```
*According to the newspaper, tomorrow is rain.*

でしょう is the opposite move. No source, no article, nobody told you anything — you looked at the sky, or you know the season, or you just have a hunch, and でしょう marks the sentence as coming from you. Swap によると for でしょう in that same sentence and the meaning shifts from "here's what I read" to "here's what I think," even though the topic never changed.

Reach for でしょう whenever you believe something but can't fully back it up — it lets you commit to an answer without overstating how sure you are. Hold onto that not-quite-certain feeling: かもしれない sits right next to でしょう on the confidence scale, for guesses that are even shakier than this one.
caution_notes: でしょう shrinks to だろう in casual speech, but だろう only fits people you'd already speak plainly to — don't use it with a teacher or stranger.
Rising-intonation でしょう？ works like a tag question, checking for agreement, not stating an uncertain guess like falling-intonation でしょう does.
でしょう states your own read on a situation; when you're passing along information from a source, によると is the right tool instead.
Drop だ before attaching でしょう to a noun or na-adjective — the copula doesn't stack on top of the ending.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are waiting at a coffee shop to meet a friend, and they are ten minutes late. You text another friend to ask if they know where he is. You need to tell them he hasn't shown up.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{mada||まだ}}{{kuru-v|te|来[き]て}}いません。
```
*He hasn't come yet.*

## How it works

To say you haven't done something *yet*, or that something hasn't happened *yet*, you use {{mada||まだ}} (which means "still" or "not yet") followed by the て form of the verb, plus {{iru-exist|nai|いない}} (or the polite {{iru-exist|masu|いません}}).

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{mada||まだ}}{{hirugohan||昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}いません。
```
*I haven't eaten lunch yet.*

Think of it as literally saying "the state of having eaten hasn't happened." Because the result of the action hasn't been achieved yet, we use the continuous state form (the て form) and make it negative.

```jp
{{ano||あの}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}は{{mada||まだ}}{{miru-v|te|見[み]て}}いない。
```
*I haven't seen that movie yet.*

```jp
{{sono||その}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}は{{mada||まだ}}{{kau-v|te|買[か]って}}いません。
```
*I haven't bought that book yet.*

## Didn't do vs. Haven't done yet

This one trips people up a lot. Why not just use the regular past tense negative to say you haven't done something?

In Japanese, the past negative means the window of opportunity is firmly closed. The event is over. If you say `宿題をしませんでした` (I didn't do the homework) to a teacher, it sounds like "I didn't do it, and I'm not going to."

If you want to imply that you still plan to do it—that the window is still open—you must use the {{mada||まだ}}〜ていない pattern.

```jp
{{mada||まだ}}{{shukudai||宿[しゅく]題[だい]}}を{{suru|te|して}}いません。
```
*I haven't done the homework yet.*

> Always use {{mada||まだ}}〜ていない if there is still a chance the action will happen. Using the simple past negative can accidentally sound defiant!

## Casual speech

In casual Japanese, speakers constantly drop the い in ていない. The pattern shrinks down to てない.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}は{{mada||まだ}}{{okiru|te|起[お]きて}}いない。
```
*My friend hasn't woken up yet.*

While the written sentence above keeps the い, in actual conversation with friends you will almost exclusively hear the contracted version: {{mada||まだ}}{{okiru|stem|起[お]き}}てない.

## Connecting it up

Right now, you're learning how to talk about things that haven't happened yet. Soon, you'll learn the exact opposite pattern: {{mou||もう}}〜ました (already did). Together, these two patterns will let you coordinate schedules, check on tasks, and make plans naturally. Keep {{mada||まだ}} in your back pocket until then!
caution_notes: Use まだ〜ていない instead of the simple past negative if there is still a chance the action will happen.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're meeting a friend at the station to catch a train, but you realize you forgot to buy your ticket. You start to apologize and say you need to go to the machine, but your friend smiles and hands you a piece of paper. They want to say, "I already bought the ticket."

When an action is completely done and dusted, you need a way to express *already*. In Japanese, that job belongs to a tiny, powerful word: もう.

## How it works

To say you already did something, simply drop もう into the sentence and put your verb in the past tense (ました). It usually sits right before the object or the verb itself.

```jp
もう{{kippu||切[きっ]符[ぷ]}}を{{kau-v|masu|買[か]いました}}。
```
*I already bought the ticket.*

```jp
{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}はもう{{owari||終[お]わり}}ました。
```
*The movie already ended.*

Because もう is just a modifier for the verb, it floats quite freely in the sentence. As long as it comes before the action it modifies, it sounds perfectly natural.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}はもう{{kaeru-v|masu|帰[かえ]りました}}。
```
*He already went home.*

## Rules and exceptions

> **Watch your endings!** If you use もう with a present/future tense negative verb, it stops meaning "already" and starts meaning "not anymore".

This trips everyone up at least once. If you say `もう食べました`, you are saying "I already ate." But if you say `もう食べません`, you are saying "I won't eat anymore." Keep your verbs firmly in the past tense (ました) when you want to talk about things you have *already* done.

## Contrast: done vs. not yet

You learned {{mada||まだ}}〜て{{iru-exist|nai|いない}} for talking about things you haven't gotten around to yet. These two patterns are exact mirror images of each other. 

When someone asks if you finished a task, you will answer with one of these two forms.

```jp
もう{{shukudai||宿[しゅく]題[だい]}}を{{suru|masu|しました}}か。
```
*Did you already do the homework?*

```jp
{{mada||まだ}}{{shukudai||宿[しゅく]題[だい]}}を{{suru|te|して}}{{iru-exist|masu|いません}}。
```
*I have not done the homework yet.*

Notice how the question uses the simple past tense ました, but the negative answer requires the continuous state form て{{iru-exist|masu|いません}}. You can't just say `まだしませんでした` (I didn't do it yet). 

Let's look at one more pair.

```jp
もう{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みました}}か。
```
*Did you already take the medicine?*

```jp
{{mada||まだ}}{{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}{{iru-exist|masu|いません}}。
```
*I have not taken it yet.*

Keep holding onto these time-related words. You know {{mada||まだ}} means "not yet", but when we eventually meet {{zenzen||全[ぜん]然[ぜん]}}〜ない, we'll see how to take a negative sentence and crank it up to "not at all".
caution_notes: Be careful: pairing もう with a negative present-tense verb changes its meaning entirely from 'already' to 'not anymore'.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're in a shop, admiring a very expensive camera. A clerk approaches and asks if you want to buy it. You want to politely let them know you're not here to spend money — you're just looking.

```jp
{{miru-v||見[み]る}}だけです。
```
*I am just looking.*

To express "only" or "just" in Japanese, you use the particle だけ. It acts as a hard boundary, fencing off whatever it attaches to and excluding everything else.

## How it works

If you want to limit a noun, you attach だけ directly to the end of it. It works like a filter, telling the listener "this thing and absolutely nothing else."

```jp
{{mizu||水[みず]}}だけ{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みます}}。
```
*I only drink water.*

```jp
千[せん]円[えん]だけ{{aru|masu|あります}}。
```
*I only have a thousand yen.*

It attaches to verbs exactly the same way. You just drop it right after the dictionary form (the plain, base form of the verb) before finishing your sentence.

```jp
{{sukoshi||少[すこ]し}}{{yasumu||休[やす]む}}だけです。
```
*I am just resting a little.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because だけ is a particle, it has to share space with the other particles you already know. This is where people usually trip up.

If you would normally mark a word with the subject marker `が` or the direct object marker `を`, だけ usually just eats them. You don't need to say `水をだけ飲みます` — just `水だけ飲みます` is perfectly natural and much more common.

But for other particles, like the target particle に, they team up. だけ usually goes right before に to say "only to" this specific person.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}だけに{{hanasu-v|masu|話[はな]します}}。
```
*I will speak only to him.*

## Contrast: The hard limit vs the outer limit

You already know まで, which sets an outer boundary ("up to" or "until"). Let's look at how まで and だけ feel side by side when you're talking about a box of snacks on the table.

```jp
{{hitotsu||一[ひと]つ}}までです。
```
*Up to one.*

```jp
{{hitotsu||一[ひと]つ}}だけです。
```
*Only one.*

With まで, you're setting a rule about the maximum allowed — zero is fine, one is fine, but stop there. With だけ, you're making a factual statement about an exact quantity. There isn't *up to* one; there is *exactly and only* one.

Hold onto this rigid, exact feeling. Right now, だけ sets a perfectly hard line. But real life is messy, and soon we'll look at ぐらい, a word that steps into the same space to soften the edges and say "about" or "roughly."
caution_notes: When combining だけ with subject (が) or object (を) particles, it usually replaces them entirely, but it stacks securely with directional particles like に.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at the convenience store to buy a nice boxed lunch, but when you look inside your wallet, you see a single 100-yen coin. It's definitely not enough. How do you express that specific feeling of "I only have this, and it's a problem"?

Enter しか (shika). When paired with a negative verb, it allows you to say "only" or "nothing but" while emphasizing that the amount or situation is limited.

## How it works

The structure is simple: **Noun + しか + Negative Verb**.

This throws a lot of learners off at first. Why use a negative verb to say you *do* have something? Think of `しか` as meaning "except for" or "other than". If you say you "don't have money other than 100 yen," you are saying there is only 100 yen.

```jp
{{saifu||財[さい]布[ふ]}}の{{naka||中[なか]}}に百[ひゃく]円[えん]しか{{aru|masu|ありません}}。
```
*I only have 100 yen in my wallet.* (Literally: Other than 100 yen, there is not.)

```jp
{{asagohan||朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]}}は{{pan||パン}}しか{{taberu|masu|食[た]べませんでした}}。
```
*I only ate bread for breakfast.*

Notice how the verb at the end is always negative (`ありません`, `食べませんでした`), even though the English translation usually sounds positive ("I have", "I ate").

## The missing particles

Just like the topic marker `は`, `しか` is a bit of a bully. When it attaches to a noun, it completely overwrites the basic object and subject particles `を` and `が`.

> You will never see `をしか` or `がしか`. The `しか` simply takes their place.

```jp
{{mizu||水[みず]}}しか{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みません}}。
```
*I drink nothing but water.* (Instead of {{mizu||水[みず]}}を)

However, other particles like `に` (location or direction) and `で` (context or action location) survive the collision. The `しか` simply stacks right after them.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{ie||家[いえ]}}でしか{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}しません。
```
*I only study at home.*

## Casual speech

When you are talking to friends, the pattern works exactly the same way, but the negative verb at the end drops into plain form (like `ない` instead of `ありません`).

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は千[せん]円[えん]しかない。
```
*I only have 1,000 yen today.*

## Contrast: Limits vs Excess

You already know how to talk about doing something *too much* with `すぎる`. Let's look at how `しか〜ない` sits at the exact opposite end of the spectrum.

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}は{{niku||肉[にく]}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}すぎました。
```
*Yesterday, I ate too much meat.*

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}は{{niku||肉[にく]}}しか{{taberu|masu|食[た]べませんでした}}。
```
*Yesterday, I only ate meat.* (And maybe I really needed vegetables.)

In both cases, you're focusing on an extreme imbalance. `すぎる` points out an excess, while `しか〜ない` points out a strict limit or a lack of something else.

Hold onto this idea of pairing a specific word with a negative verb to create a new meaning. You'll soon meet patterns like {{zenzen||全[ぜん]然[ぜん]}} (not at all), which play exactly the same game!
caution_notes: しか overwrites the particles を and が, so you will never say をしか or がしか.
The verb ending a しか sentence must always be negative, even though the English translation is usually positive.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are at a coffee shop waiting for a friend. They text you: "Sorry, the train stopped! How long will you wait?" You want to tell them you will wait for roughly an hour, but you do not want to commit to exactly sixty minutes.

```jp
一[いち]時[じ]間[かん]ぐらい{{matsu|masu|待[ま]ちます}}。
```
*I will wait for about one hour.*

## How it works

To say "about" or "approximately" in Japanese, you take a quantity and attach ぐらい (or くらい) directly to the end of it. It works with money, hours, days, or the number of things.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}は千[せん]円[えん]くらいです。
```
*This book is about one thousand yen.*

```jp
{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}三[さん]時[じ]間[かん]ぐらい{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*I study for about three hours every day.*

Notice that you can use both ぐらい and くらい. They mean exactly the same thing, and you will hear both in real life—sometimes from the same person in the same breath. ぐらい is slightly more common in modern spoken Japanese, but use whichever flows off your tongue easier.

You can also attach it to question words to ask someone for an estimate.

```jp
何[なん]時[じ]間[かん]ぐらい{{neru|masu|寝[ね]ます}}か。
```
*About how many hours do you sleep?*

```jp
八[はち]時[じ]間[かん]ぐらい{{neru|masu|寝[ね]ます}}。
```
*I sleep for about eight hours.*

## The messy time rule

Textbooks often draw a strict line with time. They say ぐらい is only for *amounts* and *durations* ("about two hours"), while you should use a completely different word for specific points on the clock ("around 3:00"). 

In casual, everyday Japanese, that rule is messy. People actually use ぐらい for specific points in time quite often.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}、三[さん]時[じ]ぐらいに{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きます}}。
```
*I will go at about three o'clock tomorrow.*

> Hold onto this exception. We will officially meet the time-marker ごろ soon, and we will untangle how it compares to ぐらい together.

## Contrast: Softening vs. Limiting

You already know だけ (only / just). These two patterns live in exactly the same slot in a sentence—right after a quantity—but they send completely opposite signals.

```jp
百[ひゃく]円[えん]だけ{{aru|masu|あります}}。
```
*I have exactly one hundred yen.*

```jp
百[ひゃく]円[えん]ぐらい{{aru|masu|あります}}。
```
*I have about one hundred yen.*

Swap だけ for ぐらい when you want to soften a number and leave yourself a little bit of wiggle room.
caution_notes: Textbook rules say ぐらい is strictly for amounts and durations, but in casual real-life Japanese, people often use it for specific times on the clock too.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are making plans to meet a friend at a coffee shop. You don't want to set a rigid, exact time because trains can be delayed or you might be running late. How do you suggest meeting "around" a certain time to keep things flexible?

## How it works

To approximate a point in time, simply attach ごろ directly after the time word. It works exactly like saying "around" or "about" in English.

```jp
三[さん]時[じ]ごろ{{eki||駅[えき]}}で{{au|masu|会[あ]います}}か。
```
*Shall we meet at the station around three o'clock?*

```jp
{{tooka||十[とお]日[か]}}ごろ{{kaeru-v|masu|帰[かえ]ります}}。
```
*I will return home around the 10th.*

```jp
{{raishuu||来[らい]週[しゅう]}}ごろ、{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kuruma||車[くるま]}}を{{kau-v|masu|買[か]います}}。
```
*I will buy a new car around next week.*

You can attach particles (little grammar markers) like に right after ごろ to lock in a specific time. However, Japanese speakers frequently drop the に in casual conversation and just say ごろ.

```jp
{{yuugata||夕[ゆう]方[がた]}}ごろに{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|masu|降[ふ]ります}}。
```
*It will rain around evening.*

## Rules and exceptions

You will sometimes see this written with the kanji 頃[ころ] (ごろ). It means the exact same thing.

There is one special case: when you want to talk about a time period in the past, like "when I was a child." Because a noun like "child" isn't a time word on its own, we connect it with the particle の, and the pronunciation usually shifts to ころ.

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}の頃[ころ]、{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{gyuunyuu||牛[ぎゅう]乳[にゅう]}}を{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みました}}。
```
*When I was a child, I drank milk every day.*

> When using ごろ with periods of life (like childhood), always remember the の and expect to hear 頃[ころ] (ころ).

## ごろ vs. ぐらい

This one trips everyone up the first week — that's normal. You already learned that ぐらい (or くらい) also means "about" or "approximately."

Here is the golden rule: ごろ is for a **point in time** on the clock or calendar (when something happens). ぐらい is for an **amount** or **duration** (how long it takes or how much of something there is).

Compare these two sentences:

```jp
二[に]時[じ]ごろ{{neru|masu|寝[ね]ます}}。
```
*I will sleep around two o'clock.*

```jp
二[に]時[じ]間[かん]ぐらい{{neru|masu|寝[ね]ます}}。
```
*I will sleep for about two hours.*

If you swap them, it sounds very strange. You cannot sleep for "two o'clock," and you cannot go to bed at "two hours." Keep ごろ on the clock, and ぐらい on the stopwatch.

You now have the tools to make flexible plans. Hold onto this idea of softening your sentences — it becomes very important when we meet patterns like {{demo||でも}} (or something) later on to make gentle suggestions!
caution_notes: Use ごろ strictly for a point in time (like three o'clock), while ぐらい must be used for an amount or duration of time (like three hours).
When attaching to a noun to mean 'around the time I was a...', use the particle の and expect the pronunciation to shift to 頃 (ころ).

items.explanation_markdown:
Japanese culture values politeness and often relies on soft, indirect ways to say no. You might say something is 'a little difficult' when you really mean it is impossible. But there are times when being indirect just does not work. When you need to make a firm, undeniable statement that something is absolutely *not* the case, you need a stronger tool.

You are sitting in a restaurant with a Japanese friend, and they just ordered a notoriously spicy dish for you to try. They watch you take the first bite, looking a bit nervous. "Is it too spicy?" they ask. You want to reassure them. You don't just want to say "It's not spicy." You want to say "It's not spicy *at all*."

To completely deny something, to drop the degree or amount down to absolute zero, you need `全然` (zenzen).

`全然` is an adverb that essentially means "completely" or "entirely." But here is the critical catch: in standard, textbook Japanese, you only ever use it to modify something that is negative.

When you pair "completely" with a negative ending, the translation becomes "not at all." You are saying that the presence of that thing—whether it is spiciness, understanding, or money—is completely non-existent.

## Emphasizing the negative

Because `全然` is just an adverb, it does not change its shape. It simply floats in your sentence, usually sitting right in front of the verb or adjective you want to negate. All the actual grammar work happens at the end of the sentence.

Let's start with adjectives. If you want to say something is not spicy at all, you first take the adjective `辛い` (spicy). You conjugate it into the negative form by dropping the final `い` and adding `くない`, which gives you `辛くない`. Then, you just place `全然` in front of it.

```jp
全[ぜん]然[ぜん]{{karai|nai|辛[つら]くない}}です。
```
*It is not spicy at all.*

The feeling here is absolute. You are not just saying the spice level is low; you are saying the spice is zero. When native speakers say this, they often put a slight vocal stress on `全然` itself to really drive the point home. Try saying it out loud: *zenzen karakunai*. You can feel how it gives the sentence a natural rhythm and punch.

This pattern works exactly the same way with verbs. You take the verb you want to negate, change it to its negative form (like the `ない` form or the polite `ません` form), and place `全然` before it.

If your teacher asks if you understand a difficult kanji, and your mind is completely blank, you use the negative polite form of `分かる` (to understand), which is `分かりません`.

```jp
{{kanji-word||漢[かん]字[じ]}}が全[ぜん]然[ぜん]{{wakaru|masu|分[わ]かりません}}。
```
*I do not understand the kanji at all.*

You can also use this to talk about things that are physically missing or completely absent. To talk about existence, you use `ある` for inanimate objects. The negative of `ある` is simply `ない` (or `ありません` to be polite).

Let's say you are checking your wallet before walking into a convenience store, and you realize it is completely empty.

```jp
{{okane||お金[かね]}}が全[ぜん]然[ぜん]ないです。
```
*I have absolutely no money.*

Notice that `全然` does not replace any particles. In the sentence above, the subject particle `が` stays exactly where it belongs. The adverb just slips in between the particle and the verb.

## Talking about the past

You can also use this pattern to talk about things that happened—or rather, completely failed to happen—in the past.

When you do this, `全然` remains exactly the same. The time-traveling happens entirely at the end of the sentence, where you conjugate your verb or adjective into the past-negative form.

Imagine a friend recommended a new movie to you. You went to the cinema to see it, but you thought it was incredibly boring. When they ask you how it was, you conjugate `面白い` (interesting) into the past-negative `面白くなかった`.

```jp
{{ano||あの}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}は全[ぜん]然[ぜん]{{omoshiroi|nai|面白[おもしろ]くなかった}}です。
```
*That movie was not interesting at all.*

The emotion is very strong here. It was a complete waste of time.

## The messy reality of modern slang

Now we have to talk about how this word actually behaves in the wild.

If you spend any time around native speakers, especially anyone under the age of fifty, you are going to hear something that violently breaks the rule I just taught you. You are going to hear people use `全然` with positive words.

Someone might ask if it is okay to sit next to you on a train, and a native speaker might reply with `全然いいです` (It is completely fine). Or they might eat something delicious and exclaim `全然おいしい` (This is totally delicious).

> **Wait, didn't you just say it has to be negative?** Yes. In strict, traditional grammar, `全然` must pair with a negative word. But language evolves, and over the last few decades, using `全然` as a general-purpose amplifier meaning "totally" or "completely" has become incredibly common in casual speech.

So, what should you do? For exams, written documents, and talking to your boss, strictly follow the rule: `全然` requires a negative verb or adjective. But when you are hanging out with friends, be prepared to hear it paired with positive words. Just know that if you use it that way yourself, you are officially using modern slang.

Another trap to avoid: you cannot just say "全[ぜん]然[ぜん]" on its own to answer a question, unless you are speaking in extremely casual, fragmented shorthand. In a polite conversation, you must finish the sentence with the negative verb or adjective.

## Dropping the politeness

Because `全然` is all about raw emphasis and emotion, it shows up in casual speech constantly. When you are speaking casually with your friends, you simply use the short, dictionary form of the negative verb or adjective. You drop the polite `です` or `ます`.

Imagine a friend asks if you are busy today, and you have absolutely nothing on your schedule.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は全[ぜん]然[ぜん]{{isogashii|nai|忙[いそが]しくない}}。
```
*I am not busy at all today.*

Or maybe someone asks if your younger brother studies at home. You want to emphasize that he absolutely does not open a single book.

```jp
{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}は{{ie||家[いえ]}}で全[ぜん]然[ぜん]{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}しない。
```
*My younger brother does not study at home at all.*

In very casual speech, you might even hear people contract the negative endings further, like turning `分からない` into `分かんない`. So `全然分かんない` (I totally don't get it) is a phrase you will hear constantly in anime or casual street interviews. The rule remains the same: the adverb amplifies the negative ending, no matter how much that ending gets shortened.

## Contrast: The absolute versus the restricted

Let's put this pattern next to something you already know. You have already learned how to use `しか〜ない` (only / nothing but).

Both of these grammar points are special because they are magnets for the negative form. The moment you use `全然` or `しか` in a sentence, you are locking the end of your sentence into a negative conjugation. But they do vastly different things to the meaning.

Look at these two sentences about eating vegetables.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}しか{{taberu|masu|食[た]べません}}。
```
*I eat nothing but vegetables.*

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を全[ぜん]然[ぜん]{{taberu|masu|食[た]べません}}。
```
*I do not eat vegetables at all.*

The `しか` sentence is restrictive. Think of `しか〜ない` as drawing a tiny circle around the one thing you *do*, and putting everything else outside the circle. You are actively doing the action of eating, but you are artificially limiting the scope to *only* vegetables. The negative ending `食べません` is not saying "I don't eat"—it is saying "I don't eat (anything else)."

The `全然` sentence is absolute destruction. Think of `全然〜ない` as erasing the board entirely. You are taking the action of eating vegetables and reducing it to zero. The negative `食べません` is literal here: you do not do the action, not even a little bit.

Also, look closely at the particles. `しか` is powerful enough that it actually destroys and replaces the normal object particle `を`. But `全然` is just a well-behaved adverb, so the `を` particle stays exactly where it normally belongs.

You can also contrast this absolute zero with the extreme upper limit you learned previously: `すぎる` (too much). These two patterns sit on complete opposite ends of the spectrum.

If you are looking at a shirt in a store and the price is outrageous, you would use `すぎる`.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{shatsu||シャツ}}は{{takai-adj|stem|高[たか]}}すぎます。
```
*This shirt is too expensive.*

But if the shirt is incredibly cheap, surprisingly so, you drop the degree of expense down to zero.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{shatsu||シャツ}}は全[ぜん]然[ぜん]{{takai-adj|nai|高[たか]くない}}です。
```
*This shirt is not expensive at all.*

Using `全然` makes your Japanese sound incredibly natural because it adds emotional weight and confidence to your denials. It turns a flat, robotic "no" into a definitive "absolutely not." Hold onto this feeling of modifying the degree of a negative—it will come in handy when you meet its softer cousin `あまり〜ない` (not very much) soon.
caution_notes: While you will hear native speakers use 全然 with positive words in modern slang (like 全然いい), strict grammar requires it to pair with a negative word.
Do not use 全然 entirely on its own to answer a question in formal speech; always finish the sentence with the negative verb or adjective.

items.explanation_markdown:
You just walked out of a movie with a friend. They turn to you and ask if you liked it. You didn't hate it, but it certainly wasn't a masterpiece. How do you soften the blow and say it wasn't *very* good?

You use あまり.

```jp
{{sono||その}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}はあまり{{omoshiroi|nai|面白[おもしろ]くない}}です。
```
*That movie isn't very interesting.*

## How it works

あまり is an adverb—a word that sits right before the adjective or verb you want to modify. But here is the golden rule: **あまり must always pair with a negative word.**

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}はあまり{{samui|nai|寒[さむ]くない}}です。
```
*Today is not very cold.*

It works exactly the same way for actions. If you don't do something very often or very much, just place あまり before the negative verb.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}はあまり{{niku||肉[にく]}}を{{taberu|masu|食[た]べません}}。
```
*I do not eat meat much.*

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}はあまり{{neru|masu|寝[ね]ませんでした}}。
```
*I didn't sleep much yesterday.*

## The conversational shortcut

When speaking casually, あまり almost always morphs into あんまり. It means the exact same thing, but adding that little bounce in the middle makes it flow better in fast speech.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}はあんまり{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}しません。
```
*He doesn't study much.*

## Contrast: The negative spectrum

You already know {{zenzen||全[ぜん]然[ぜん]}} (not at all). Both of these words require a negative verb or adjective to finish the sentence, but they sit at different ends of the spectrum.

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}はあまり{{muzukashii|nai|難[むずか]しくない}}です。
```
*Japanese is not very difficult.*

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}は{{zenzen||全[ぜん]然[ぜん]}}{{muzukashii|nai|難[むずか]しくない}}です。
```
*Japanese is not difficult at all.*

Use あまり when you want to soften a statement, and {{zenzen||全[ぜん]然[ぜん]}} when you want to completely deny it.

> **Don't fall into the affirmative trap:** Because English speakers often think of words like "much" as positive ("I ate very much"), it is incredibly tempting to throw あまり into a positive sentence. Don't do it. A sentence like `あまり食べます` (literally: "I eat not much") sounds broken to a Japanese speaker. The verb itself must carry the negative state: you *do not* eat much.

Keep this scaling pattern in your back pocket. Soon you'll learn how to say things *become* a certain way using {{naru-become||なる}}, and knowing exactly how to measure your descriptions will make you sound much more natural.
caution_notes: あまり must always be paired with a negative verb or negative adjective.
Do not use あまり in affirmative sentences to mean 'very much'.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're hanging out with a friend and they look a bit tired. You want to offer them a drink, but asking "Do you want tea?" can sometimes feel a little too direct. You want to offer tea as just one casual option among many. How do you say "How about tea or something?"

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}でも{{dou||どう}}ですか。
```
*How about some tea or something?*

You might have already encountered this word as a way to say "but" at the start of a sentence. But when you attach it directly to the end of a noun, it does a completely different job. It becomes a soft suggestion marker, meaning "or something".

## How it works

To use it, just take a noun and add でも right after it. You'll almost always follow this up with an invitation or a question.

```jp
{{koohii||コーヒー}}でも{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みません}}か。
```
*Would you like to drink coffee or something?*

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}、{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}でも{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ません}}か。
```
*Shall we watch a movie or something this weekend?*

By adding this to your sentence, you are throwing out an idea without locking the listener into it. It makes your invitation feel much softer and more considerate, giving the other person an easy out if they prefer to do something else.

## Rules and exceptions

When you attach this to a noun, it eats the object particle `を`. You will hear people say {{koohii||コーヒー}}でも, but never `コーヒーをでも`. It completely replaces the particle.

> Be careful: this pattern is strictly for suggestions, invitations, or offering choices to others. If you use it to state your own firm plans, it sounds apathetic or dismissive, like "I guess I'll just have coffee since there's nothing better." Keep it for offering things to friends or making group plans!

```jp
{{kouen||公[こう]園[えん]}}でも{{aruku|masu|歩[ある]きません}}か。
```
*Shall we walk in the park or something?*

## Casual speech

When you are talking to close friends, you don't need all the polite `ませんか` machinery. You can just use the dictionary form of the verb with a rising intonation to suggest doing something.

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}でも{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}}？
```
*Want to drink tea or something?*

## Contrast: Suggesting vs Limiting

Let's look at how this changes the vibe of your sentence compared to a particle you already know: だけ (only).

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}でも{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}}？
```
*Want to drink tea or something?*

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}だけ{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}}？
```
*Do you want to drink ONLY tea?*

The first one is a warm, open-ended offer. The second one sounds like you are checking a strict limitation. They occupy the exact same spot in the sentence, but do completely opposite jobs!

Next time you want to invite someone out, try throwing in an "or something" to keep things breezy.
caution_notes: It completely replaces the object particle を, so never say をでも.
Using this for your own actions instead of an invitation makes you sound dismissive, like "I guess I'll just do this."

items.explanation_markdown:
Modern life is full of overlapping actions. We rarely do just one thing at a time—we listen to music on our commute, we talk with friends over dinner, and we clean our rooms while thinking about our weekend plans. In English, we tie these simultaneous activities together with the word "while."

In Japanese, describing two actions happening at the exact same time requires a structural shift in how you build your sentence. Instead of relying on a separate conjunction word like "while," Japanese relies on the grammatical suffix ながら. 

By attaching ながら to a verb, you create a sturdy bridge that connects two continuous actions seamlessly. In this lesson, we will explore exactly how to construct these sentences, understand which of your two actions takes grammatical priority, and navigate the strict rules Japanese imposes on who is allowed to perform them.

## How it works: Building the bridge

Japanese grammar values consistency, especially when connecting multiple ideas. To link two verbs together with ながら, we cannot simply smash their dictionary forms together. We need a specific connector, and for this pattern, that connector is the **verb stem**.

What is a verb stem? It is the polite `ます` form of a verb, simply with the `ます` chopped off. It acts as an open puzzle piece, waiting for a grammatical suffix to attach to it.

Let's walk through how to isolate the stem and attach ながら across the different verb groups:

**Group 1 (U-verbs)**
Take the verb {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} (to drink). First, change it to its polite form: {{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みます}}. Next, drop the `ます`, leaving you with the stem: `飲み`. Finally, attach the suffix to get {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]み}}ながら (while drinking).
- {{aruku||歩[ある]く}} (to walk) → {{aruku|masu|歩[ある]きます}} → {{aruku|stem|歩[ある]き}} → {{aruku|stem|歩[ある]き}}ながら (while walking)
- {{kaku||書[か]く}} (to write) → {{kaku|masu|書[か]きます}} → {{kaku|stem|書[か]き}} → {{kaku|stem|書[か]き}}ながら (while writing)

**Group 2 (Ru-verbs)**
Take the verb {{taberu||食[た]べる}} (to eat). The polite form is {{taberu|masu|食[た]べます}}. Remove `ます` to isolate the stem `食べ`, and attach the suffix to get {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}ながら (while eating).
- {{miru-v||見[み]る}} (to watch/see) → {{miru-v|masu|見[み]ます}} → {{miru-v|stem|見[み]}} → {{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}ながら (while watching)

**Irregular Verbs**
Take the verb {{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}} (to study). The polite form is {{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します. The stem is simply `勉強し`. Attach the suffix to get {{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}しながら (while studying).
- {{sanpo-suru||散[さん]歩[ぽ]する}} (to take a walk) → {{sanpo-suru|masu|散[さん]歩[ぽ]します}} → {{sanpo-suru|stem|散[さん]歩[ぽ]し}} → {{sanpo-suru|stem|散[さん]歩[ぽ]し}}ながら (while taking a walk)

Once you have your first verb modified, you simply follow it up with your second verb to complete the sentence.

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]み}}ながら{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|masu|読[よ]みます}}。
```
*I read a book while drinking tea.*

```jp
{{ongaku||音[おん]楽[がく]}}を{{kiku-v|stem|聞[き]き}}ながら{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*I study while listening to music.*

## The Three Absolute Rules

While the construction of this pattern is mechanically simple, using it naturally requires adhering to three strict linguistic rules. Breaking these rules is a common trap for learners, as English does not share these exact constraints.

### 1. The final verb is the "boss"

In English, the sentences "I eat while I watch TV" and "I watch TV while I eat" mean practically the same thing in casual conversation. In Japanese, however, the two halves of a ながら sentence are not equal. 

The final verb—the one at the very end of the sentence—carries the ultimate grammatical and contextual weight. It is your primary action. The verb attached to ながら is merely a background activity or a secondary descriptor of *how* you are doing the main action.

Let's observe how swapping the verbs completely changes the focus of the sentence:

```jp
{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}ながら{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|masu|食[た]べます}}。
```
*I eat a meal while watching TV.*

In this first sentence, eating is the main event. You are sitting at the table, focused on your meal, and the television simply happens to be on in the background.

```jp
{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}ながら{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ます}}。
```
*I watch TV while eating a meal.*

In this second sentence, watching the television is your primary activity. Perhaps you are engrossed in a movie on the couch, and you are casually snacking on food as a secondary action.

Why does this hierarchy matter? Imagine a police officer ({{keikan||警[けい]官[かん]}}) asks what you were doing. You would want your main, purposeful action to land firmly at the end of the sentence. Your listener will always interpret the final verb as your core objective.

### 2. The single-subject guarantee

> The most common mistake learners make is trying to use ながら to describe two different people doing two different things.

This pattern fuses two actions so tightly together that they must belong to a single biological entity or actor. You can only use it when the *exact same person* is performing both the first action and the second action.

You can easily say "I study while I listen to music" because you are the sole actor. However, you absolutely cannot use ながら to say "I study while my friend watches TV." If you attempt to attach two different subjects to the two halves of the sentence, the Japanese listener will become profoundly confused, assuming one person is somehow performing both actions. To describe two different people doing things at the same time, Japanese relies on entirely different grammatical structures.

### 3. Time travels to the end

This grammar pattern is a chameleon when it comes to time. The suffix ながら is completely neutral—it does not know if an action happened yesterday, is happening today, or will happen tomorrow. 

The tense of the entire sentence is anchored exclusively by the final verb. If you want to talk about an overlapping action that occurred in the past, you **do not** put the first verb into the past tense. The stem remains completely frozen, and the final verb does all the heavy lifting.

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}、{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}と{{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]し}}ながら{{aruku|masu|歩[ある]きました}}。
```
*Yesterday, I walked while talking with a friend.*

Notice that we do not say `話しましたながら`. The stem `話し` stays exactly as it is, while the final verb `歩きました` tells the listener that the entire event happened in the past.

```jp
{{byouin||病[びょう]院[いん]}}で{{zasshi||雑[ざっ]誌[し]}}を{{yomu|stem|読[よ]み}}ながら{{matsu|masu|待[ま]ちました}}。
```
*I waited at the hospital while reading a magazine.*

## Action verbs vs. Instantaneous verbs

Because this pattern describes two things happening simultaneously over a period of time, it logically requires verbs that actually take time to perform. It pairs perfectly with continuous action verbs like reading ({{yomu||読[よ]む}}), washing ({{arau||洗[あら]う}}), walking ({{aruku||歩[ある]く}}), and singing ({{utau||歌[うた]う}}).

```jp
{{utau|stem|歌[うた]い}}ながら{{souji-suru|masu|掃[そう]除[じ]します}}。
```
*I clean while singing.*

Conversely, it does not work well with instantaneous verbs—actions that happen in a split second and are immediately over. You cannot naturally pair it with verbs like {{owaru||終[お]わる}} (to finish), {{shimeru||閉[し]める}} (to close), or {{ochiru||落[お]ちる}} (to drop/fall). For instance, saying "While dropping my wallet, I walked" creates a logical clash, as dropping happens in an instant and cannot serve as a continuous background activity.

## Casual speech: Formality at the finish line

Just as the final verb dictates the tense of the sentence, it also dictates the formality. Because Japanese relies heavily on the end of a sentence to establish social distance, the first half of a ながら sentence stays completely untouched in casual speech.

To make the sentence casual, you simply change the final polite `ます` verb into its plain dictionary form. The stem + ながら remains identical.

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]み}}ながら{{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}}。
```
*I talk while drinking tea. (Casual)*

Whether you are speaking formally to a teacher ({{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}) or casually to a close friend ({{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}), the first half of your multitasking sentence will look exactly the same.

## Contrast: Untangling time-related grammar

As you expand your ability to describe complex sequences of events, it is incredibly easy to mix up grammar patterns that sound similar in English. Let's establish clear boundaries between simultaneous actions and sequential actions.

### Simultaneous vs. Sequential: ながら vs. てから

You have already learned how to use てから to say "after doing" something. Let's contrast these two patterns using a scenario: You arrive at a hotel ({{hoteru||ホテル}}) and want to inspect your room.

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]み}}ながら{{heya||部屋[へや]}}を{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ます}}。
```
*I look at the room while drinking tea.*

By using ながら, these actions overlap. You are physically holding the teacup in your hand, taking sips as you walk around inspecting the room.

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}を{{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}から{{heya||部屋[へや]}}を{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ます}}。
```
*After drinking tea, I look at the room.*

By using てから, the actions are strictly sequential. You finish the entire cup of tea, set the cup down, and only then do you begin walking around the room. The actions do not overlap for even a single second.

### Strictly Simultaneous vs. Broad Timeframes: ながら vs. とき

You also know how to use とき to mean "when" or "at the time of." While "when" and "while" feel similar, their rules are very different. とき simply sets a broad scene or timeframe, and crucially, it allows for different subjects to perform different actions.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}}とき、{{ie||家[いえ]}}で{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|masu|読[よ]みます}}。
```
*When it rains, I read a book at home.*

In this sentence, the rain ({{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}) is doing the falling, and you ({{watashi||私[わたし]}}) are doing the reading. Because there are two entirely different actors, using ながら here is grammatically impossible. 

## Wrapping up

Mastering how to describe overlapping actions is a massive step forward in conversational fluency. Remember to find your verb stem, add the suffix, guarantee that only one person is performing both actions, and place your most important action at the very end of the sentence.

Right now, you are learning how to connect actions based on time. Soon, you will learn how to connect actions based on purpose—using patterns like ため(に) to say "I study in order to go to a foreign country." But for today, grab a drink, sit back, and practice your new grammatical multitasking.
caution_notes: The action placed at the very end of the sentence is always the main focus or primary activity.
Both actions connected by this pattern must be performed by the exact same person.
The tense and formality of the entire sentence are determined entirely by the final verb; the first verb remains frozen in its stem form.
items.mnemonic_text: Toto the turtle rides one of his sample doors over <reading>Niagara</reading> Falls. He never looks up from his newspaper: reading <grammar>while falling</grammar>, the whole way down. {{shinbun||新聞}}を{{yomu|stem|読み}}<reading>ながら</reading>{{ochiru||落ちる}}。

items.explanation_markdown:
Have you ever noticed how often we look for validation in our daily conversations? When we experience something interesting, surprising, or pleasant, our first instinct is usually to share it with someone else. We don't just want to state a flat fact; we want the person next to us to agree, to feel the same way, and to share in the moment. When we see a beautiful sunset, eat an amazing meal, or experience something shocking, the experience feels incomplete until someone else nods and says, "Yes, exactly!"

Imagine you are walking down the street with a friend and you see a surprisingly tall tree. You could simply say, "That tree is tall." But in English, you are much more likely to say, "That tree is tall, isn't it?" or "Look, it's tall, right?" You are checking in with your friend to make sure they are seeing what you are seeing.

In Japanese, this social glue—this desire to confirm shared realities and seek agreement—is extremely important. It shows empathy, builds connection, and makes your spoken Japanese sound incredibly natural and conversational. You have already learned how to state simple facts using `です`. You also know how to state that something is not the case using `ではありません` or its more casual sibling `じゃないです`.

But what happens when you want to take a positive statement and turn it into a question that expects a friendly "yes" from your listener? To do this, you will use the pattern `じゃないですか`.

Let's dive into how this powerful, highly common phrase works, and how you can start using it to connect with the people around you.

## How it works

The mechanics of this grammar point are wonderfully simple. The structure is quite literal if you break it down: you are taking a plain form sentence and adding `じゃない` (the plain negative, meaning "is not") followed by `ですか` (the polite question marker).

Literally, you are asking "Is it not [X]?" But just like in English, this is a rhetorical question. You are actually saying, "It IS [X], don't you agree?"

Because this pattern attaches to the entire thought that comes before it, the conjugation rules are very straightforward. You simply take the plain form of whatever word ends your statement, and attach `じゃないですか` directly to it. The plain form, as you may recall, is the casual, dictionary-style form of a word. It strips away the polite wrappers like `です`, leaving only the core grammatical structure.

Let's look at how this attaches to the four main types of words in Japanese: Nouns, Na-adjectives, I-adjectives, and Verbs.

**1. Attaching to Nouns**

When you want to seek agreement about a noun, you simply take the bare noun itself. You do not use `だ` or `です` before the pattern. Notice how clean and simple this is. There is no need for complicated particle maneuvering. You are directly attaching the rhetorical question to the core subject.

```jp
{{are||あれ}}は{{gakkou-v||学[がっ]校[こう]}}じゃないですか。
```
*That is a school, isn't it?*

In this scenario, perhaps you and your friend were looking for the school, and you suddenly spot it in the distance. You point it out, expecting them to agree and confirm that yes, you have finally found it.

**2. Attaching to I-Adjectives**

Because Japanese adjectives contain their own state of being, they are incredibly versatile. I-adjectives are very easy here because their plain form is just the dictionary form you already know (ending in "i"). Do not add `です` in the middle; just put the adjective right next to the pattern.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}、{{atsui-obj||熱[あつ]い}}じゃないですか。
```
*This tea is hot, isn't it?*

Imagine you both take a sip of the tea at the same time and burn your tongues slightly. You look at your friend and say this, expecting them to nod vigorously in agreement.

**3. Attaching to Na-Adjectives**

Just like nouns, Na-adjectives drop any final `だ` or `です` when connecting to this pattern. You use the "stem" of the adjective (the base word itself).

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{machi-v||町[まち]}}は{{nigiyaka||賑[にぎ]やか}}じゃないですか。
```
*This town is lively, isn't it?*

You step off the train into a new town, and immediately hear music, see lots of people, and feel the bustling energy. You turn to your travel companion and make this enthusiastic observation.

**4. Attaching to Verbs**

For verbs, you use the plain dictionary form. It does not matter if the verb is a physical action or a state of being; the plain form connects directly.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{hashiru||走[はし]る}}じゃないですか。
```
*He runs every day, doesn't he?*

Here, you and a friend might be talking about a mutual acquaintance, and you bring up his daily running habit to support a point you are making about his health or dedication.

**The Formal Variation**

You will sometimes hear a slightly stiffer, more formal version of this pattern: `ではないですか`. While `ではないですか` means exactly the same thing, the use of `では` instead of `じゃ` elevates the register. 

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{jisho||辞[じ]書[しょ]}}は{{benri||便[べん]利[り]}}ではないですか。
```
*This dictionary is convenient, isn't it?*

You might encounter this formal variation in literature, on the news, or when someone is speaking passionately in a formal debate. For your everyday conversations, however, the standard `じゃないですか` will be your best friend.

## Rules and exceptions

While this pattern is very useful, it has a few sharp edges that you need to be careful with. Understanding these nuances will prevent awkward misunderstandings.

> **Intonation changes everything!** To seek agreement, your voice must **rise** at the end of the sentence, just like a standard question.

In English, tone of voice can completely change the meaning of a sentence, and Japanese is no different here. If you let your voice drop or stay flat at the end of `じゃないですか`, the meaning shifts slightly. Instead of seeking agreement ("Isn't it?"), a flat or dropping intonation sounds more like pointing out a fact the listener should already know, or even a mild correction ("Look, it is, you know"). For now, focus on the rising intonation to keep your statements friendly and collaborative.

> **This is NOT a true negative question.**

This is the most common trap for learners. Because the phrase contains `じゃない` (the negative form of the copula), it is very tempting to use it when you genuinely want to ask if something is missing, broken, or untrue. Let's make this crystal clear.

For example, if you are looking at a movie and you sincerely want to know if it is boring or uninteresting, you **cannot** use `面白いじゃないですか`. If you say that, you are actively stating that you think it IS interesting! To ask a genuine negative question (e.g., "Is it not interesting?"), you have to conjugate the adjective itself into the negative form (which we will practice in later lessons). Remember: `じゃないですか` as a fixed phrase confirms a **positive** belief.

Finally, keep in mind the politeness level. Even though this pattern ends with the polite `ですか`, the core of the phrase uses the casual plain form `じゃない`. Because of this mix, it has a friendly, conversational tone. It is perfectly fine to use with colleagues, acquaintances, and friendly strangers, but you should avoid using it with highly respected superiors or in very formal business situations, as it can sound a bit too familiar.

## Casual speech

Because Japanese is highly adaptable to social situations, you can easily alter this pattern for casual conversations with your close friends, family, or romantic partners.

To do this, you simply drop the `ですか` at the end. What remains is just `じゃない`.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}、{{omoshiroi||面[おも]白[しろ]い}}じゃない。
```
*This movie is interesting, isn't it?*

When using the casual `じゃない` to seek agreement, the rising intonation at the end becomes absolutely critical. If you say `面白いじゃない` with a flat tone, it sounds more like a statement of unexpected discovery ("Oh, this movie is actually interesting"). With the rising tone, it becomes the friendly "Right? Isn't it interesting?" that you are looking for.

## Contrast

When learning a new language, the hardest part isn't necessarily memorizing the new words, but figuring out how the new words fit in with the ones you already know. It is very easy to confuse this new pattern with grammar you have already mastered. Let's look at two minimal pairs to see exactly how swapping the grammar changes the meaning of the sentence.

**Contrast 1: Statements of Negative Fact**

You already know `ではありません`, which is the standard, polite way to negate a noun. Compare these two sentences:

```jp
{{ano||あの}}{{hito||人[ひと]}}は{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}では{{aru|masu|ありません}}。
```
*That person is not a teacher.*

```jp
{{ano||あの}}{{hito||人[ひと]}}は{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}じゃないですか。
```
*That person is a teacher, isn't he?*

In the first sentence, you are stating a cold, objective fact: the person's profession is not teaching. In the second sentence, you firmly believe the person IS a teacher, and you are asking your listener to confirm it with you.

**Contrast 2: Guessing vs. Pointing Out**

You also know `でしょう`, which is used to make a guess or seek agreement. So what is the difference between `でしょう` and `じゃないですか`?

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}の{{tesuto||テスト}}は{{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}でしょう。
```
*Tomorrow's test will be difficult, right?*

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}の{{tesuto||テスト}}は{{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}じゃないですか。
```
*Tomorrow's test will be difficult, won't it?!*

When you use `でしょう`, the tone is softer. It feels like you are making a prediction and gently asking if the other person shares that prediction. It translates well to a softer "right?" or "probably".

When you use `じゃないですか`, the emotion is stronger. You are pointing out a strong reality that you believe to be true, and almost demanding that the listener recognize it too. It has a feeling of "Look at the facts, obviously it will be difficult, don't you agree?!"

By mastering these subtle differences, you take a massive step toward fluency. You are no longer just sharing cold information; you are actively inviting people into your perspective and building shared realities.
caution_notes: Always use a rising intonation at the end of the sentence to show you are seeking agreement.
Do not use this pattern to ask a genuine negative question; it is a positive statement looking for validation.
Because it combines casual plain forms with polite markers, avoid using this pattern with highly respected superiors.

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are sitting at your desk, textbooks open, working hard on a beautiful weekend afternoon. A friend calls and asks why you aren't out relaxing. You want to express that you have a driving goal behind your hard work. You aren't just studying randomly; you are studying *in order to* achieve something specific. 

In English, we use phrases like "in order to" or "for the sake of" to explain the motivations, ambitions, and reasons behind our actions. In Japanese, this vital function is handled by the pattern `ために`. 

Learning this grammar point is a massive step forward in your conversational ability. It transitions you from simply describing what is happening in the world, to explaining the dreams and purposes that drive those actions. Whether you are saving money for a car, studying for a difficult test, or cooking a healthy meal for your family, `ために` allows you to communicate your underlying purpose clearly.

Before we look at the specific rules, we need to uncover a structural secret about Japanese grammar that will make this pattern incredibly easy to remember and use naturally. 

The word `ため` is actually a noun. 

Historically, it translates to "benefit," "advantage," "sake," or "purpose." When you understand that `ため` is simply a noun, you do not have to memorize any complex new conjugation rules. You already know exactly how to connect other words to nouns! Furthermore, the `に` that follows it is simply the target particle you already know—the exact same one you use to point toward a time or a physical destination. By saying `ために`, you are literally saying "pointing toward the purpose of X." Let's look at how this applies when we build sentences with verbs and nouns.

## How it works: Connecting Verbs

When you want to say "in order to do [Action]," you must attach the verb directly to `ために`. Because `ため` acts as a noun, we just use the plain, standard Dictionary Form of the verb. 

```jp
{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}へ{{iku-v||行[い]く}}ために、{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*I am studying Japanese in order to go to Japan.*

Why do we strictly use the Dictionary Form? Why not the past tense? To understand this, you have to think about the logical flow of time. 

A purpose or a goal is inherently something that has not been completed yet at the time you take the action. If you are studying to go to Japan, the act of "going to Japan" is a future event relative to your current studying. Because it is an unfulfilled future goal, it must take the present/future tense, which is the Dictionary Form.

```jp
{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kuruma||車[くるま]}}を{{kau-v||買[か]う}}ために、{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}を{{suru|masu|します}}。
```
*I will work in order to buy a new car.*

You can never use the past tense here. Saying `買ったために` (past tense) to mean "in order to buy" makes no logical sense in Japanese, because you cannot aim for a goal that has already been completed. The goal must always remain in the forward-looking Dictionary Form.

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{naru-become||なる}}ために、{{daigaku||大[だい]学[がく]}}で{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*I will study at the university in order to become a teacher.*

## How it works: Connecting Nouns

Often, your purpose is not an action, but a specific person or a thing. You work *for your family*. You read books *for the test*. 

Since we established that `ため` is a structural noun, how do we connect two nouns together in Japanese? We use the linking particle `の`. In English, we say "for my family" and the word "for" acts as a preposition attaching directly to the noun. Japanese does not have prepositions; it uses particles to build relationships. 

Just as you would use `の` to say `私の車` (my car), you use it to say `家族のため` (family's sake). The particle `の` acts as a bridge of association between the two nouns.

```jp
{{kazoku||家[か]族[ぞく]}}のために、{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{hataraku|masu|働[はたら]きます}}。
```
*I work every day for the sake of my family.*

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}のために、{{oishii||おいしい}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}を{{tsukuru|masu|作[つく]ります}}。
```
*I will make a delicious meal for the sake of my child.*

```jp
{{tesuto||テスト}}のために、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|masu|読[よ]みます}}。
```
*I will read a book for the test.*

## Rules and exceptions

Japanese grammar is remarkably sensitive to human intention. Some grammatical structures care deeply about whether you are a passive observer of an event, or the active pilot making the event happen. 

`ために` demands that you be the pilot. 

> You can only use `ために` with "volitional" actions—meaning actions that you have conscious, deliberate control over.

You can consciously decide to go to Japan (`行く`), you can decide to buy a car (`買う`), and you can decide to study (`勉強する`). These are all volitional actions, so they work perfectly with this grammar pattern. 

However, you cannot use `ために` with things that are outside of your direct control, such as the weather, automatic states, or potential abilities. For instance, raining is not a volitional human action. Therefore, you cannot say `雨が降るために` to mean "in order for it to rain." When you want to talk about non-volitional states or things happening naturally, Japanese uses a completely different pattern that you will encounter later in your studies. For now, remember this golden rule: if you are using `ために`, you must be in the driver's seat of the action.

Another important nuance to keep in mind is subject consistency. Usually, the person holding the goal in the first half of the sentence is the exact same person doing the action in the second half. If the sentence is "In order to buy a car, I work," it is inherently understood that *I* am the one buying the car and *I* am the one working.

## Casual speech: Dropping the に

Up until now, we have explored this grammar point in its full, complete form. However, in both casual everyday conversation and in slightly more formal writing (such as essays or news articles), the particle `に` is frequently dropped, leaving just `ため`.

```jp
{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}のため、{{kamera||カメラ}}を{{kau-v|masu|買[か]いました}}。
```
*I bought a camera for the trip.*

```jp
{{okane||お金[かね]}}のため、{{hataraku|masu|働[はたら]きます}}。
```
*I work for money.*

Dropping the `に` does not change the core meaning of the sentence at all. It simply tightens the rhythm. In spoken Japanese, dropping it makes the sentence flow a bit faster and sound slightly more relaxed and conversational. In written Japanese, stripping away extra particles can make sentences feel crisper and more objective. 

As a learner, it is completely safe and grammatically perfect to always use the full `ために`, but you should begin training your ear to recognize the shorter `ため` when native speakers use it in rapid conversation.

## Contrast: ために vs ので

Because `ために` tells us *why* we are doing something, it is very easy for English speakers to confuse it with `ので` (because), which you have already learned. In English, we sometimes get sloppy and use the words "because" and "for" almost interchangeably. In Japanese, these two concepts are fundamentally different and face in opposite directions.

`ので` is backward-looking. It describes a cause or a reason that is already an established fact, and then gives the resulting action. It represents a strict sequence of cause and effect.

`ために` is forward-looking. It describes a destination, an ambition, or a goal that has not happened yet, and then gives the action required to get there. It represents purpose and effort.

Let's look at how swapping these two grammar points completely changes the feeling and reality of a sentence, even using the exact same vocabulary.

```jp
{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}へ{{iku-v||行[い]く}}ので、{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*Because I am going to Japan, I study Japanese.*

In this first sentence using `ので`, the trip to Japan is an established, factual cause. The plane tickets are likely already booked, and the trip is definitely happening. The trip is the cause that forces you to study.

```jp
{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}へ{{iku-v||行[い]く}}ために、{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*In order to go to Japan, I study Japanese.*

In this second sentence using `ために`, the trip to Japan is a dream or a goal. It is not an established fact yet. You are actively studying to make the ambition a reality. 

## Contrast: ために vs {{mae||前[まえ]}}に

Finally, let's briefly compare this with another pattern that connects to the Dictionary Form of verbs: `前に` (before).

```jp
{{neru||寝[ね]る}}{{mae||前[まえ]}}に、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|masu|読[よ]みます}}。
```
*Before I sleep, I read a book.*

Both patterns attach directly to the plain Dictionary Form. However, `前に` is purely about the chronological order of the clock. It simply states that Action A happens, and then Action B happens later on the timeline. It contains no emotion or motivation. 

`ために`, on the other hand, is entirely about intention. When you use it, the first action is the entire driving reason that the second action exists. It is not just about time; it is about motivation.

Mastering `ために` gives your Japanese a whole new layer of depth. Keep your goals clearly focused in the dictionary form, remember the linking `の` when dealing with nouns, and you will sound incredibly natural when sharing your motivations with the world!
caution_notes: Always use the dictionary (present) form of verbs before ために, never the past tense, because a goal is always in the future relative to the action.
You can only use ために with volitional actions that you have conscious control over, not for natural states or things outside your control.
Do not confuse ために (forward-looking purpose) with ので (backward-looking cause); they express completely different motivations.
